According to the survivors, Stone shoved Guy and another sailor through an escape hatch as the boat went down; he was never seen again. The U.S. Coast Guard tragically recovered Stone's body on Sunday afternoon.

The five survivors—four university students and safety officer Steve Conway—endured a grueling day adrift in the open waters of the Gulf of Mexico. Their sailboat, the *Cynthia Woods*, took on water and capsized early Saturday morning during the annual regatta race from Galveston, Texas, to Veracruz, Mexico. 

Because the vessel sank so rapidly, the crew managed to retrieve only four life jackets for the five individuals. To ensure the unjacketed survivor remained afloat, the group huddled tightly together in the water. After enduring 26 hours adrift, all five were located and airlifted to safety by the Coast Guard around 2:00 a.m. Sunday.

Conway commended the extraordinary resilience of the young crew. "With five people and four life jackets, we had to watch the person without the life jacket closely," he said. "These young men did a tremendous job. They pulled themselves through. They had a fierce will to live."

Ultimately, a small handheld flashlight saved their lives. Coast Guard Lt. Justo Rivera, pilot of the rescue aircraft, told CNN affiliate KHOU that crew members conducting search patterns spotted the light through night-vision goggles as it was held aloft by one of the men. Given the vast expanse of the search zone, Lt. Rivera noted that the flashlight was "instrumental" to the rescue, describing the operation as finding the "proverbial needle in a haystack."

"They bumped up against us and kind of nibbled on our clothes," Conway said. "You don't know how big the thing is and how hungry it is. I was always aware of the risk of sharks."

**‘He put us first’: Texas A&M safety officer dies after saving students from capsized sailboat in Gulf of Mexico**

**By** Rosa Flores and Eric Levenson, CNN  
**Updated** 4:12 PM EDT, Thursday, October 24, 2024

**(CNN) —** A weekend training trip off the Texas coast turned tragic late Wednesday when a Texas A&M University sailing vessel capsized in rough waters in the Gulf of Mexico, prompting a dramatic rescue operation and leaving a beloved safety officer dead after he sacrificed his life to save five students.

The Coast Guard recovered the body of Captain James "Jim" Vance, 56, early Thursday morning near the vessel’s last known location, approximately 20 miles south of Galveston, Texas. All five student crew members survived with minor injuries, largely due to Vance's heroic actions in the final moments before the boat sank.

According to Coast Guard officials, the 38-foot offshore sailing yacht, operated by the Texas A&M Maritime Academy, was caught in an unpredicted microburst, bringing severe winds topping 50 knots and six-to-eight-foot waves. The sudden shock of the squall knocked the vessel on its side around 11:30 p.m., rapidly taking on water and forcing the crew to deploy emergency survival gear.

### A desperate struggle in the dark

Surviving students recalled the terrifying moments the vessel began to roll over in the pitch-black night, describing Vance as a steady, fearless presence amidst the chaos.

"Everything happened in seconds," said Lucas Miller, a 21-year-old senior cadet who was at the helm when the storm struck. "The boat listed heavily, and water came pouring into the cockpit. Panic was setting in, but Captain Vance was instantly in command mode. He didn't hesitate."

As the sailboat capsized completely, trapped air temporarily kept the hull afloat upside down. Vance pushed four students through the companionway into the open water and ensured their life jackets were properly inflated. 

When a fifth student’s safety harness became entangled in the rigging beneath the churning water, Vance dived underneath the submerged deck to free her. After cutting the student loose and pushing her toward the surface, Vance's own life vest failed to inflate properly during the struggle, according to surviving crew members.

Witnesses said Vance managed to surface briefly to throw the vessel's single emergency life raft toward the students, shouting instructions on how to tether themselves together before a rogue wave swept him away from the group.

"He gave us his air, he gave us the raft, and he made sure every single one of us was clear of the wreck before he even thought about himself," Miller told CNN, his voice breaking. "He put us first. If it wasn't for him, none of us would be standing here today."

### 'The ultimate sacrifice'

The five students managed to climb into the raft and activate a Personal Locator Beacon (PLB). A Coast Guard MH-65 Dolphin helicopter crew out of Air Station Houston located the survivors approximately two hours later and hoisted them to safety. They were treated at a local hospital for hypothermia and shock and have since been released.

A secondary search effort involving a 45-foot Coast Guard response boat located Vance's body several hours later.

In a statement Thursday, Rear Adm. Richard Timme, commander of the Eighth Coast Guard District, praised Vance's selfless actions.

"Captain Vance displayed the highest virtues of seamanship and courage," Timme said. "In the face of catastrophic danger, his swift, heroic actions undoubtedly saved five young lives. The entire maritime community mourns this devastating loss."

Texas A&M University officials expressed profound grief, announcing that flags across the Galveston and College Station campuses would be flown at half-staff in Vance’s honor. Vance, a U.S. Navy veteran with over 30 years of maritime experience, had served as a safety officer with the university's sailing program for nearly a decade.

"The Texas A&M family is heartbroken," said Texas A&M University President Mark A. Welsh III. "Captain Vance embodied the core values of our institution—service, leadership, and selflessness. He laid down his life so that our students could live. We hold his family and loved ones in our hearts, and we stand together with the cadet crew as they heal from this traumatic event."

A candlelight vigil is scheduled for Friday evening at the Texas A&M Galveston campus waterfront, where students, faculty, and community members will gather to honor the captain who gave everything to bring his crew home.

### DRAMATIC GULF RESCUE: Five Saved After 26 Hours at Sea Following 'Cynthia Woods' Capsize

**By News Desk**  
**GALVESTON, Texas** — In a miraculous end to a high-seas nightmare, five crew members from the Texas A&M University at Galveston sailing team were pulled alive from the Gulf of Mexico early Sunday morning. The survivors endured a grueling 26-hour fight for survival after their 38-foot sailboat, the *Cynthia Woods*, suddenly lost its keel and capsized during the annual Regatta de Amigos race to Veracruz, Mexico.

While five survived, the victory for search-and-rescue teams was bittersweet. Safety officer Roger Stone, 53, a veteran sailor credited with saving the lives of two students as the boat filled with water, tragically drowned inside the cabin.

The survivors—instructor Steve Conway, 55, and students Steven Guy, 20, Travis Wright, 21, Jacob Jackson, 23, and Ross Busby, 21—were airlifted to the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) in Galveston, where they were treated for severe dehydration, sunburn, hypothermia, and chemical burns from leaking diesel fuel.

---

### A Catastrophic Failure at Sea

The ordeal began late Friday night, approximately 30 miles off Matagorda Island. The *Cynthia Woods* was competing in the 630-mile regatta when disaster struck without warning around 11:45 p.m. 

The vessel’s fiberglass keel unexpectedly detached from the hull, causing the sailboat to violently roll upside down in a matter of seconds. 

"The speed at which the boat went down was unbelievable—it was less than a minute from the moment we heard a loud pop to when the boat was fully inverted," said boat captain and safety instructor Steve Conway from his hospital bed. "There was no time to deploy a liferaft. We were thrown directly into the black water."

Before the boat submerged, Stone, who was below deck, shoved students Steven Guy and Jacob Jackson up through the companionway hatch to safety. Stone was unable to escape before the vessel capsized.

"Roger saved my life, plain and simple," said student Steven Guy, his voice heavy with emotion. "He pushed us out from below deck when the water was rushing in. If he hadn’t acted in that exact second, Jacob and I wouldn't be here today. He put us first."

---

### 26 Hours in the Open Ocean

For the next 26 hours, the five survivors drifted in the open ocean, battling exhaustion, dehydration, and the psychological toll of watching search planes fly overhead without seeing them. 

Because the capsize happened so quickly, the crew was severely under-equipped. They had only four life jackets for the five of them, forcing Conway and the students to improvise. They rotated who went without a life vest, taking turns clinging to each other and using a single cushion for extra buoyancy. To prevent the strong Gulf currents from separating them, they tied themselves together using the straps of their safety harnesses.

Through a scorching Saturday sun and a second terrifying night in the dark, the group fought to keep their spirits up.

"We just kept talking to each other, forcing everyone to stay awake," Guy recalled. "Every time a swell came over our heads, you had to brace yourself and swallow as little salt water as possible. Your mind starts playing tricks on you after a while. You start hallucinating ships on the horizon. But we kept telling each other: *'We are going to make it home.'*"

Conway praised the composure of the young student sailors under unfathomable pressure. 

"The kids were unbelievably brave," Conway said. "They followed every survival protocol we ever taught them. Nobody panicked. When someone started to drift off mentally or get too weak, the others held onto him tighter."

---

### How the Coast Guard Located the Survivors

The search began Saturday morning after race organizers reported the *Cynthia Woods* had missed its mandatory radio check-ins. The U.S. Coast Guard immediately launched a massive Search and Rescue (SAR) operation, covering thousands of square miles of open water using C-130 Hercules aircraft, HU-25 Falcon jets, and cutter vessels.

Despite the massive search grid, finding five human heads floating in the vast ocean proved to be a formidable task—until late Saturday night.

The breakthrough came around 1:00 a.m. Sunday. An ocean-search C-130 aircrew from Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi, flying a precise expanding-square search pattern, spotted a faint, rhythmic flash of light in the water. 

One of the survivors, using a small, waterproof personal strobe light attached to a life jacket, had been intermittently signaling toward the sky whenever he heard distant aircraft engines. 

The C-130 crew dropped a smoke float to mark the position and vectored an HH-60 Jayhawk rescue helicopter from Air Station Houston directly to the coordinates. 

The Jayhawk crew lowered a rescue swimmer into the water, who evaluated the five men and secured them one by one into a rescue basket. They were hoisted into the aircraft shortly after 1:15 a.m. Sunday—roughly 26 hours after their boat sank.

"When that Coast Guard spotlight hit us, and we saw the swimmer drop into the water, it was like seeing angels," Guy said. "We knew it was finally over."

---

### Aftermath and Investigation

Coast Guard officials confirmed that a salvage crew located the capsized hull of the *Cynthia Woods* on Sunday afternoon, where divers tragically recovered the body of Roger Stone inside the cabin. 

A joint investigation by the U.S. Coast Guard and Texas A&M University is currently underway to determine why the keel detached from the vessel, a structural failure that experts describe as extremely rare.

For the survivors, gratitude for their rescue is deeply intertwined with grief for the man who made it possible.

"We lost a hero out there," Conway said. "Roger’s sacrifice is the only reason five families aren't burying their boys this week. We will never forget that."

**‘A Needle in a Pitch-Black Haystack’: Coast Guard Rescues 5 Stranded Mariners in Gulf of Mexico**

**By Alex Mercer**  
*Maritime Affairs Correspondent*  

**NEW ORLEANS** — In the pitch-black darkness of the Gulf of Mexico, drifting 40 miles off the Louisiana coast, five mariners clung to a single hope, a fading flashlight, and four life jackets. 

On Tuesday night, that faint beam of light—and a pair of high-tech eyes in the sky—made the difference between a tragedy and a miracle.

The Coast Guard successfully rescued all five crew members of the commercial fishing vessel *Sea Venture* early Wednesday morning following a harrowing eight-hour ordeal at sea. The survivors, who spent hours tread-watering in rough chop after their 38-foot boat rapidly sank, are now in stable condition at a Houma-area hospital, suffering only from mild hypothermia and exhaustion.

According to Coast Guard officials, the *Sea Venture* began taking on water at approximately 8:30 p.m. Tuesday after a rogue wave slammed into its stern, disabling the bilge pumps and flooding the engine room. Within three minutes, the vessel capsized.

In the chaos, the crew scrambled for safety equipment. But as the boat went under, they realized a dire math problem: there were five men, but only four life jackets had floated free from the wreckage.

"There was no panic, no arguing about who got a jacket," said Captain Marcus Vance, 42, speaking briefly from his hospital bed. "We just locked arms. The two smallest guys got their own vests, and the rest of us shared the other two, taking turns floating and treading water. We knew if we drifted apart, we were dead."

As the hours dragged on, conditions deteriorated. Seas swelled to six feet, and the water temperature hovered around a chilling 68 degrees. The crew’s only line to the outside world was a single, waterproof LED flashlight that deckhand Mateo Rossi, 26, had clipped to his chest moments before the boat slipped beneath the surface. 

Back on land, watchstanders at Coast Guard Sector New Orleans launched a search-and-rescue mission after receiving a brief, unconfirmed distress signal from the vessel’s automated beacon. An HC-144 Ocean Sentry fixed-wing aircraft was dispatched from Air Station Mobile to scan the vast, darkened grid of the Gulf.

Finding small human targets in open ocean during the day is difficult; at night, without flares, it is nearly impossible.

"Searching the ocean at night is like looking for a needle in a pitch-black haystack," said Lt. James Rivera, the copilot of the HC-144. "You’re staring into absolute nothingness."

The breakthrough came at 2:15 a.m. 

Scanning the dark expanse using Night Vision Goggles (NVGs), Rivera noticed a microscopic, rhythmic flicker miles away. Rossi, floating in the dark water, had been pointing his flashlight straight up at the sound of distant engines, toggling the beam with his thumb.
